author: Kyas Williamson
title: Blockbusters: Good Will Hunting Opinion | Blockbusters: Good Will Hunting
text:
This review contains spoilers.
The extensive math equations in this film remind me of the exact reason I chose to be an English major. Shoutout to Weinberg’s foundational disciplines for allowing me to evade math courses.
Before this column, I’d never watched “Good Will Hunting.” The idea of reviewing a film I had no prior knowledge of was daunting. What if I lacked any opinion on the movie and didn’t have time to choose another topic? I can’t hide behind movies I’ve seen before forever, so I decided to branch out and give this one a shot.
Will Hunting (Matt Damon) is an orphaned janitor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology whose life changes when he solves an impossible equation. Due to a physical altercation, Will is faced with jail time and could lose his opportunity to succeed. To qualify for parole, Will must study under Professor Gerald Lambeau (Stellan Skarsgård), who pushes Will to the level of young genius he never achieved.
Another caveat to Will’s parole is required therapy sessions. Will believes he doesn’t need therapy, so he resists it. He psychologically embarrasses psychologist after psychologist – whether that be claiming they’re gay or singing in their sessions – acting as if it’s some game. Desperate to keep Will under his watch, Lambeau turns to his college roommate, Sean Maguire (Robin Williams), as a last resort.
The movie’s first act moves at a glacial pace. Before Will and Maguire met, the film feels directionless. While their first meeting is eventful, the second one reels Will into their new partnership.
Will’s character shines throughout his sessions with Maguire. For starters, he casually refers to Maguire as “Sean” and excessively curses. I did not find the cursing pleasant, not because I don’t like cursing, but because it perpetuates the stereotype that cursing is something members of a lower class do. The only characters in the film that curse are from lower-class upbringings.
Aside from the questionable stereotype, Will’s background is relatable. He cycles through the same few shirts throughout the entire film, which is the first time I’ve seen a movie reuse outfits as people do in real life. He balances work and his studies under Lambeau. He tackles challenging coursework and homework. He goes out with friends. He’d fit right in at Northwestern.
The highlight of the film is the comparison between Will, Sean and Lambeau. The two adults foil each other, yet they share a pain that beautifully establishes their motives for directing Will’s future. One achieved success too late; the other never reached his full potential. Will represents the pair at the beginning of their journeys. He’s yet to make choices that will sway the direction of his future.
The adults’ shortcomings influence their differing approaches, which they constantly fight over, to guiding Will’s future. Lambeau aims to turn Will into everything he never was, while Sean wants Will to discover himself.
Skarsgård’s performance as Lambeau is phenomenal. Even though the character doesn’t necessarily want what’s best for Will’s well-being, Skarsgård’s acting choices display Lambeau’s internal struggle between care for Will and his ache to turn Will into everything he was not. Skarsgård perfectly brought to light Lambeau’s pain of not being good enough through his overbearingness towards Will and his scenes lashing out at Sean.
Speaking of Sean, Williams was a generational talent. The magic he produced leapt from the screen into my heart. I found myself getting emotional at every monologue, connecting to every heartbreak and soaking in every word of wisdom. Williams plays the mentor character exceptionally well, perfectly capturing the gentleness, security and guidance of a mentor.
The pair act against each other stunningly, showcasing the years of resentment, hurt and love they’ve built for the other.
The emotional payoff in the third act moved me to tears. In particular, the relationship between Will and Sean was wonderfully executed by the actors, and the callbacks to earlier moments in the film were delightful. The final shot — which I won’t spoil— is a beautiful landscape that left me feeling hopeful.
This film is about honing one’s potential, connecting with people and reaching out for help when it’s needed. NU students are the best of the best, but that doesn’t make them indestructible. Some people may come from a similar background to Will’s and feel similarly that they do not need help. I would encourage us all to learn from Will’s mindset change that help is for everyone.
Typically I would dive deeper into spoilers, especially about the film’s ending, but I believe those who haven’t seen it and read this column should experience the ending spoiler free. I urge you to watch this film and hope you resonate with it the same way I did.
Kyas Williamson is a Weinberg first-year and author of “Blockbusters” He can be contacted at kyaswilliamson2030@u.northwestern.edu.
